implementation_notes: The JDK ships the pattern: ServiceLoader.load(Iface.class) locates provider classes named in META-INF/services/<iface> (or declared with a module's uses/provides directives), instantiates them lazily, caches them and exposes stream() for inspection before instantiation. Application code refers only to the service interface, so implementations can be added by putting a jar on the class path - the declarative form replaces the hand-written locator for pluggable providers. Use findFirst()/stream().filter(...) when several providers exist and the choice needs a rule, and prefer it over JNDI or container lookups whenever the binding is a class-path fact rather than a deployment name.
pitfalls: Providers need a public no-arg constructor; a malformed provider file or a missing class surfaces as ServiceConfigurationError only when the iterator is advanced, so a broken jar can look healthy until first use.
Iteration order is unspecified: selecting "the first provider" must be a deliberate rule (filter on an annotation or a priority), not luck.
ServiceLoader objects obtained via the thread context class loader must not be cached VM-wide - container and application-server deployments leak class loaders that way.

variants.name: JNDI InitialContext lookup
variants.implementation_notes: The J2EE form the pattern was named for: the client obtains an InitialContext (or an injected @Resource reference) and looks objects up by JNDI name, while a locator class hides context creation, caches the context and the looked-up factories, and returns the expected interface (JNDI hands back Object, so the cast is unchecked unless you go through a checked wrapper such as Spring's JndiTemplate.lookup(name, Class)). Keep it where the runtime is the naming service - application servers, LDAP, CORBA - and the binding name is a deployment concern; bind names in descriptors rather than hard-coding them, cache the context, and close it when the component shuts down.
pitfalls: lookup returns Object, so a wrong binding is an unchecked ClassCastException at the use site (and a wrong-but-assignable binding only fails later, on first use); wrap the lookup in one place that validates the type.
Every lookup throws the checked NamingException, so each use site needs exception plumbing that a constructor parameter would not have needed.
Cached contexts and factory objects must be released on shutdown; a context kept forever holds naming-provider connections.

variants.name: Spring ApplicationContext.getBean
variants.implementation_notes: A DI container doubles as a locator because ApplicationContext inherits getBean from BeanFactory, so a framework-created object can pull collaborators by type or name instead of being wired. Spring's own style is constructor injection; keep getBean for code Spring did not construct (container-created filters and listeners, legacy integration, ApplicationContextAware hooks) and for prototype lookups where every call must return a fresh instance. Annotate lookup-only components as lazy or resolve inside the method rather than the constructor when the bean may be created before the context is refreshed.
pitfalls: getBean resolves eagerly on first call and throws NoSuchBeanDefinitionException or NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at that moment - not at startup, where the graph would have been validated.

Request- and session-scoped beans resolved outside a request (background thread, thread pool) fail with IllegalStateException: no thread-bound request found; resolve them through a scoped proxy or inside the request.
Looking up beans by name ties code to bean ids that are configuration, not contracts; prefer the typed overload with the interface.
